title: NRS Information Circular No. 2026/10: Taxation of Non-Resident Persons Engaged in Shipping and Air Transport

pages.text:
NIGERIA INLAND REVENUE SERVICE
PLOT 1241, KUR MOHAMMED AVENUE, CENTRAL AREA, ABUJA, NIGERIA
INFORMATION CIRCULAR
NO: 2026/10 PUBLICATION DATE: 29TH JUNE, 2026
Subject: TAXATION OF NON-RESIDENT PERSONS ENGAGED IN
SHIPPING AND AIR TRANSPORT
This circular is issued for the information and guidance of taxpayers, tax
practitioners and the public in line with the provisions of the relevant tax
laws. The circular withdraws and replaces FIRS Information Circular No.
2023/11 of 29th December 2023.
1.0 Introduction
This Circular explains how the relevant provisions of the Nigeria Tax Act,
2025 and the Nigeria Tax Administration Act, 2025 apply to non-resident
shipping and airline operators. It sets out the basis for determining
assessable and total profits, clarifies the tax treatment of freight and non-
freight income, the impact of tax treaties, compliance obligations, and the
tax implications of leasing or chartering ships and aircraft. In addition, it
provides guidance on ancillary services, employment income exercised
aboard ships or aircraft, and the carriage of crude oil from Nigeria. The
Circular does not apply to Nigerian resident companies engaged in shipping
or air transport.
2.0 Scope
This Circular applies to taxation of income derived from Nigeria by non-
resident persons engaged in shipping or air transport and does not apply to
Nigerian resident engaged in similar trade or business.
3.0 Income from shipping and air transport business in Nigeria
3.1 Classification of income from shipping and air transport in
Nigeria
The profits derived by a non-resident company from airline or shipping
operation within Nigeria may fall into two categories; freight income or non-
freight income.
(1) Freight income refers to income earned from the carriage of passengers,
mails, livestock or goods loaded into an aircraft or ship in Nigeria,
1

excluding transhipment.
(2) Non-Freight income refers to income earned from other business
activities including but not limited to commission, demurrage, container
clearing fees, container damage fees, rental of ship or aircraft,
stevedoring, etc.
3.2 Taxation of freight income
The following rules govern the taxation of freight income derived by non-
resident
companies from the operation of ship or air transport businesses in Nigeria:
Where a non-resident person carries on the business of transport by sea or
air, and any ship or aircraft owned, leased or chattered by it calls at any
port in Nigeria, the:
(a) profits arising from the carriage of passengers, mails, livestock or
goods shipped, or loaded into a ship or an aircraft in Nigeria (freight
income) is liable to tax;
(b) profits arising from carriage of passengers, mails, livestock or goods,
which are brought to Nigeria solely for trans-shipment are not
chargeable to tax in Nigeria;
(c) tax is levied on the profits attributable to such Nigerian operations,
irrespective of the company’s country of incorporation; and
(d) tax base for the taxation of freight income of foreign airline or shipping
companies is the “total profits” computed based on the relevant
provisions of the law.
3.2.1 Determination of total profits where there is similar tax
treatment
Where the Service is satisfied that the tax jurisdiction of residence of a
non-resident shipping or air transport company computes and assesses
tax on a basis not materially different from that of Nigeria, the total profits
of the non-resident company will be determined as follows:
(a) The profits or losses attributable to Nigerian operations are
calculated using the following ratios:
(i) “Global Adjusted Profit Ratio”: The ratio of the company’s profits
or losses (before depreciation allowances) for an accounting
period to its gross revenue derived from the carriage of
passengers, mails, livestock, or goods.
Global Adjusted Profit Ratio = Adjusted Profits or losses
Gross revenue from carriage activities
2

(ii) “Global Depreciation Ratio” The ratio of the company’s
depreciation allowances for an accounting period to its gross
revenue from the carriage of passengers, mails, livestock, or
goods.
Global Depreciation Ratio = Depreciation allowances
Gross revenue from carriage activities
(b) Total profits will be determined as follows:
(i) “Assessable Profit” is calculated by applying the global adjusted
profit ratio to the freight revenue (total income derived from the
carriage of passengers, mails, livestock, or goods shipped or
loaded in Nigeria).
(ii) “Depreciation Allowance” is determined by applying the global
depreciation ratio to the Nigerian-sourced freight revenue.
(iii) “Total Profit” is derived by deducting the depreciation allowance
from the assessable profits.
Note:
To provide the required satisfaction to the Service, the non-resident company
should submit to the Service, a copy of its published account and a statement
containing the following information and certified by the tax authority of its
country of residence:
(i) Gross revenue from carriage activities,
(ii) Computation of the Adjusted Profits or losses, showing the addition
of depreciation back to the accounting profits and other tax
adjustment to the profits,
(iii) Depreciation Allowance, and
(iv) Declaration or an attestation stating that the information contained
in the certificate is true and correct.
3.2.2 Situation of non-similar tax treatment
Where the provisions of paragraph 3.2.1 cannot be satisfactorily
applied, the total profit to be subject to tax in Nigeria will be determined
by applying the ratio of Earnings Before Interest and Tax (EBIT) to total
income or revenue (profit margin) to the turnover attributable to
Nigeria.
NOTE:
(i) the information required for the computation of the ratio of EBIT to total
income or revenue is as disclosed in the company’s audited financial
3

statements,
(ii) where the company does not have published financial statements for the
relevant period, or is not required to publish such statements, the profit
margin will be determined by the Service by reference to the published
financial statements of a comparable company.
3.2.3 Deemed total profit
Where at the time of assessment, the total profit cannot, for any reason,
be ascertained using any of the approaches described in paragraphs
3.2.1 and 3.2.2, the Service will determine the total profit by applying
a fair percentage to the gross revenue derived from the carriage of
passengers, mail, livestock, and goods shipped from or loaded in
Nigeria.
3.3 Minimum tax
Notwithstanding the approaches described in paragraph 3.2 above, the tax
payable should not be less than 2% of the total revenue from the carriage of
passengers, mails, livestock or goods shipped or loaded in Nigeria.
Where the tax computed is less than 2% of the total revenue receivable from
the carriage of passengers, mails, livestock or goods shipped or loaded in
Nigeria, the tax payable will be the 2% of the total revenue receivable from
the carriage of passengers, mails, livestock or goods shipped or loaded in
Nigeria.
Illustration 1
The global income statement of NAM Airways Inc., a foreign airline which
operates into Nigeria for the year ended 31st December 2026 shows the
following:
$’000 $’000
Income from passengers, cargo and mails:
Outside Nigerian Sales 3,100,000
Nigerian sales 100,000
Global Transportation Revenue 3,200,000
Transportation Expenses:
Salaries and other expenses 2,300,000
Depreciation 320,000
Other disallowable expenses 180,000 (2,800,000)
4

Net Transportation Profit 400,000
Other Income:
Income from Properties (net) 25,000
Income from operating maintenance 50,000
hanger (net)
Income from duty-free shops (net) 50,000
Income from catering (net) 75,000 200,000
Net profit 600,000
NAM Airways has two ground staff in Nigeria and 5% of the ‘other income’ is
attributable to the operation of the Airline in Nigeria. Assume that the
provisions in the tax law of the home country of NAM Airways Inc is similar to
that of Nigeria with respect to the computation of assessable profits.
Treatment
a. To determine the Nigerian tax payable on freight income
i. calculate the profit on the transportation business: $’000
Net transportation Profit as per account 400,000
Add Depreciation 320,000
Other disallowed expenses 180,000
Global Transportation Assessable Profits 900,000
ii. Compute relevant statutory ratios:
(a) Global Adjusted Profit ratio:
900,000 x 100%
3,200,000 = 28%
(b) Global Depreciation ratio: 320,000 x 100%
3,200,000 = 10%
iii Compute the tax payable on the freight income:
Nigerian freight income as above
100,000
Total Assessable Profits 28% of $100,000 =
5

28,000
Less: Depreciation Allowance 10% of $100,000 =
10,000
Total Profit 18,000
Tax at 30% = 5,400
(iv) Minimum tax (2% of the Nigerian sales) = 100,000 X 2% = 2,000
Therefore, Tax Payable on freight income = 5,400
Note:
Depreciation allowance is in lieu of capital allowance granted under the First
Schedule to NTA.
b. To determine the Nigerian tax payable on non-freight income
$’000
Total or global non-freight income (net) 200,000
Amount attributable to Nigeria (5% X 200,000) = 10,000
Tax @ 30% (30% X 10,000) = 3,000
Note:
For non-freight income, the tax payable will be 4%
of the non-freight income generated from Nigeria,
except where WHT above 4% has been applied. In
such case, the WHT will be the final tax.
C. To determine the Total Tax Liability in Nigeria:
Tax payable on freight income 5,400
Tax payable on non-freight income 3,000
Total Tax Liability in Nigeria 8,400
Illustration 2: Alternative Profit Computation
Consider Transco Cargo Inc., a US-based shipping company, which generates
$20 million in revenue from transporting goods loaded in Nigeria. The ratio of
EBIT to total income derived from the company’s financial statement is 10%.
The global adjusted profit and depreciation ratios could not be applied because
the rules applicable by the US tax authority in computing and assessing the
profit of the non-resident company to tax are different from that of Nigeria.
Treatment:
The taxable profit is calculated as follows:
 Nigerian revenue: $20 million.
 Profit margin: 10%.
 Total profit = $20 million × 10% = $2m
6

 Tax @ 30% = $600,000.00
3.4 Tax Treaty Situation
The existing Articles on Shipping and Air Transport in the Double Taxation
Agreements (DTAs) between Nigeria and other countries deals with the
sharing of taxing right between Nigeria and the treaty partners. The Articles
moderate the provision of Section 18 of NTA as regards sum receivable from
the international carriage of passengers, mails, livestock or goods shipped or
loaded in Nigeria. The scope of the Articles covers only international traffic
(i.e. the place of departure is Nigeria, while the place of arrival is outside
Nigeria or vice versa). Consequently, the Articles do not deal with profits
derived by a non-resident company from domestic routes (i.e. where place
of departure and arrival are in Nigeria). The explanations in this paragraph
are applicable regardless of whether the vessel or aircraft is owned, leased or
otherwise at the disposal of the Non-resident company.
There are two broad categories of Nigerian DTAs as regards the treatment of
companies engaged in shipping or air transport. These are DTAs that grant
unconditional tax exemption to shipping companies or airlines of tax treaty
partners and those that provide only conditional (based on reciprocity)
exemption.
3.4.1 Unconditional tax exemption
With respect to tax treaties that grant unconditional tax exemption, the
companies engaged in shipping or air transport are exempt from
Nigerian income tax if they are residents (as defined by the DTA) of the
treaty partner and have submitted a Certificate of Residence, issued by
the treaty partner, to the Service.
3.4.2 Conditional tax exemption
With respect to DTAs that grant conditional tax exemption, treaty
benefits are granted in either of the following ways:
(a) Where there is Reciprocity:
Reciprocity clause, in the Article dealing with shipping and air transport,
means that ships operated in international traffic by Nigerian companies
call at the seaports of a treaty partner and ships operated in
international traffic by companies of the treaty partner also call at
Nigerian seaports. Similarly, it may also mean aircrafts operated in
international traffic by Nigerian companies call at the airports of a treaty
partner and aircrafts operated in international traffic by companies of the
treaty partner also call at Nigerian airports in a given year of assessment.
7

Therefore, reciprocity applies only where profits as meant in the Article,
are derived by companies or other persons of both countries from the
operation of ships or aircraft in international traffic to or from each
other.
As such, “Reciprocity” in international traffic will occur only where a
company of Nigeria derives profits from the operation of ships in
international traffic to a treaty partner, and a company of a treaty
partner similarly derives profits from the operation of ships; or a
company of Nigeria derives profits from the operation of aircraft in
international traffic to a treaty partner, and a company of a treaty
partner similarly derives profits from the operation of aircraft in
international traffic to Nigeria.
In such a case, the foreign company will not pay tax in Nigeria, and the
Nigerian company will not pay tax in the other country. The profits of
the companies will only be taxable in their respective home countries.
(b) Where there is no Reciprocity:
This is where a company of Nigeria’s tax treaty partner operates a ship
or aircraft in international traffic calling at a Nigerian port in a given year
of assessment, without any corresponding operation of any ship or
aircraft of a Nigerian company in international traffic calling at a port of
that treaty partner.
In determining reciprocity, payment made to the government of Nigeria
or any instrumentality thereof, by way of a commercial or other
agreement that does not deal with tax issues, will not be considered as
profits derived by an enterprise of Nigeria from the operation of ships
or aircrafts in international traffic, for the purpose of satisfying the
condition of reciprocity.
Consequently, the foreign company of the treaty partner is assessable
to tax in Nigeria in respect of income arising from such operations.
However, Nigerian tax shall be at the rate specified in the respective DTAs.
NOTE:
(i) The treatment agreed in the DTAs (i.e. full exemption of the foreign
company from income tax or taxation at treaty rate) is limited to the
activities specified in the tax treaty. Profits from all other activities of
the foreign company (not listed in the tax treaty) shall fall under the
Article on Business Profits in the Agreement and be taxable in Nigeria
as provided by the relevant domestic tax law.
8

(ii) for the purposes of reciprocity, ships and aircrafts are not
interchangeable, i.e. ship for ship and aircraft for aircraft.
Illustration 3:
XYZ Airlines Ltd., a foreign company resident in Utopia a treaty partner of
Nigeria, carries passengers from Abuja Nigeria to Utopia with three flights
per week.
Treatment:
This trip would be regarded as falling within the definition of international
traffic.
Illustration 4:
XYZ Airlines Ltd., a foreign company resident in Utopia, a treaty partner of
Nigeria, carries passengers from Abuja Nigeria to Utopia with three flights
per week. XYZ Airlines as part of the same voyage to Utopia, first flies
between Abuja to Lagos to pick up passengers and then continues to Utopia.
Treatment:
The first and second legs of that trip, Abuja to Lagos and Lagos to Utopia will
both be part of a voyage regarded as falling within the definition of
international traffic, because the trip of the passengers carried from Abuja did
not end in Lagos but continues to Utopia.
Illustration 5:
XYZ Airlines Ltd., a foreign company resident in Utopia, a treaty partner of
Nigeria, carries passengers from Abuja Nigeria to Utopia with three flights per
week. XYZ Airlines as part of the same voyage to Utopia, first flies between
Abuja to Lagos to pick up more passengers and then continues to Utopia. The
airline also has license to operate domestic routes on the days it is not carrying
passengers to Utopia, and to disembark in Lagos, some of the passengers it
carries from Abuja to Lagos in its flight enroute Utopia.
Treatment:
Income from the operation of domestic routes on the days it is not carrying
passengers to Utopia, as well as that from Abuja passengers disembarked in
Lagos would not be regarded as falling within the definition of
international traffic.
Illustration 6:
XYZ Airlines Ltd., a foreign company resident in Utopia a treaty partner of
Nigeria, jointly operates flights in domestic routes with ABC Nigeria Ltd. XYZ
Airlines Ltd provides the aircrafts and pilots, ABC provides the other crews
9

and other logistics.
Treatment:
Income derived from Nigeria by XYZ Airlines Ltd from a pool or joint operation
of flight in domestic routes would not be regarded as falling within the
definition of international traffic.
4.0 Tax Returns
A non-resident company involved in the carriage of passengers, mails, livestock
or goods loaded into ships or aircrafts in Nigeria is required to file monthly
returns with the Service and pay the tax computed for its operation that
month. The monthly returns shall be filed not later than the 21st day of the
following month in respect to the freight income earned from Nigeria with
evidence of payment. In addition, an annual return shall be filed with the
Service with respect to freight and non-freight income earned from Nigeria in
line with the process and procedure for filing annual income tax returns in
Nigeria.
4.1 Monthly Tax Returns
The monthly returns shall contain the following;
(a) Detailed statement of the Nigerian operations for that month showing
the amount of gross revenue;
(b) Tax Computation schedule, for tax charged at the rate of 2% of gross
revenue or at the rate specified in an applicable tax treaty;
(c) Evidence of tax payment on income derived from the carriage of
passengers, mail, livestock, or goods loaded in Nigeria.
NOTE:
The 2% on gross revenue paid is not the final tax. The payment of the 2%
of monthly revenue only enables the companies to fulfill the requirement for
repatriation of ticket sales pending the conclusion of the tax matters for the
relevant year of assessment.
4.2 Annual Tax Returns
The contents of the annual tax returns of non-resident shipping and airline
company are:
(a) the company's full audited financial statements;
(b) the financial statement of the Nigerian operations, attested to by
an independent, qualified or certified accountant in Nigeria;
(c) where a separate financial statement of the Nigerian operations
cannot be provided, the company is required to provide detailed
gross revenue statements of its Nigerian operations, certified by
one of its directors and its external auditors, and supported with
the contract agreements;
10

(d) tax computation schedules based on the profits attributable to
its Nigerian operations;
(e) a true and correct statement, in writing, containing the profits
from each and every source in Nigeria;
(f) duly completed Income Tax Self-Assessment forms;
(g) a computation of the effective tax rate and additional tax payable,
where applicable; and
(h) evidence of payment of the tax due.
Note:
(i) ’’Full audited financial statement’’ implies the global or consolidated
account of the foreign entity,
(ii) Financial statement of the Nigerian operations should include
necessary details required under the relevant domestic legislation,
(iii) Capital Allowances computation is limited to qualified capital
expenditures incurred for Nigerian operations only,
(iv) Information contained in the financial statement of the Nigerian
operations will form the basis for computing the assessable profits,
capital allowances, total profits and tax due,
(v)Income Tax self-assessment forms are available at
https://www.firs.gov.ng/TaxForms/FIRSTaxForms.
4.2.1 Computation details for Annual Returns
(a) Tax computation - the tax computation under paragraph 3.2.1 of this
Circular should disclose the following details:
(i) Global revenue (i.e. total revenue receivable worldwide from the
carriage of passengers, mails, livestock or goods),
(ii) The global net profit from the business of carriage of passengers,
mails, livestock or goods,
(iii) Tax adjustments carried out on the accounting net profit to arrive at
the adjusted profit from the business of carriage of passengers,
mails, livestock or goods,
(iv) The adjusted profit ratio from the business of carriage of
passengers, mails, livestock or goods (i.e. the ratio of the adjusted
profits to global earnings (revenue) for the period),
(v) The amount of global depreciation in respect of the business of
carriage of passengers, mails, livestock or goods for the period,
(vi) The depreciation ratio (i.e. the ratio of the annual global
depreciation to global earnings (revenue) of the business of
carriage of passengers, mails, livestock or goods for the period),
(vii) Earnings (revenue) of the company derived from the carriage of
passengers, mails, livestock or goods shipped or loaded into
aircrafts in Nigeria during the period,
11

(viii) Assessable profits of the company derived from Nigeria (i.e.
revenue of the company from Nigeria specified in (vii) above
multiplied by the adjusted profit ratio determined in (iv) above),
(ix) Capital allowance deducted (i.e. revenue of the company from
Nigeria specified in (vii) above multiplied by depreciation ratio
determined in (v) above),
(x) Total profits or full profits taxable in Nigeria (i.e. the Assessable
profits of the company computed in (viii) above less Capital
allowance computed in (ix) above),
(xi) Tax computed, which is the total profits or ‘full profits’ computed in
(x) above multiplied by 30%, and
(xii) Computation of minimum tax; and
(b) Tax payable in Nigeria, which is the higher of tax computed in (xi) and
minimum tax computed in (xii). Capital Allowances Computation – this
should contain details of depreciation charged into the global account, the
computation of depreciation ratio and capital allowances deductible in
Nigeria (computed using the depreciation ratio).
5.0 Role of Regulatory Agencies in Ensuring Tax Compliance
Regulatory agencies in the shipping, air transport, and related sectors are
required to request non-resident persons engaged in shipping and airline
operations to provide evidence of tax compliance as a pre-requisite for
conducting business or obtaining approvals or permits in Nigeria. Acceptable
evidence includes:
(i) Proof of income tax filing for the preceding tax year;
(ii) Tax Clearance Certificates demonstrating income tax payments for the
three preceding tax years; or
(iii) Evidence of tax declaration and payment for the specific carriage or
shipment activity.
Note:
A foreign airline or shipping company that carries out operation in Nigeria shall
register for tax and may obtain a TCC from the Service to meet the regulatory
requirement in paragraph (ii) above.
6.0 Income from Leasing or Charter of Ships and Aircraft
One of the common features of the Shipping and Air Transport business is
leasing of vessels, ships or aircraft. The lease may be on “time or voyage
basis”, or “demise or bare-boat basis” in the case of ships; and dry or wet
lease in the case of aircraft.
(a) A voyage or time charter: This is an arrangement in which the
charterer (or lessee) charters the ship (or part of it) for a particular
voyage in which the route and ports have been pre-determined or for
12

an agreed period of time of which they are free to sail to any port and
transport any cargo.
Voyage or time charter of ships is similar to wet lease or leasing
arrangements of aircraft. Depending on the charter arrangement, the
charterer or lessee may direct where the ship or aircraft will go but
the owner of the ship retains possession of the ship, and maintenance
of the vessel still falls under the purview of the owner. It is the owner
of the ship that remains responsible for the employment of the master
and crew and responsible for the technical operation of the vessel.
The charterer or lessee pays hire (rental fee) to the owner of the
vessel and may sometimes pay for the fuel the vessel consumes, port
charges, demurrage, commissions etc. (especially for time charter)
but does not retain ownership, while the owner will handle all
maintenance-related costs. In a time charter the commercial control
of the vessel is not handled by the owner, while in a voyage charter,
both the technical and commercial control is retained by the owner.
A voyage or time charter of ship or wet lease of aircraft mostly
constitutes an operating lease.
(b) Bareboat or demise charter: Bareboat or demise charter
arrangement has similar features as dry lease or leasing arrangement
of an aircraft. In a dry lease or bare-boat or demise charter, the
owner gives possession of the ship to the charterer, and the charterer
hires its own master, crew and ground staff. The charterer or lessee
obtains possession and full operational control of the vessel along
with the legal and financial responsibility for it. The charterer or lessee
pays for all operating expenses, including fuel, crew, port expenses
and insurance. A bareboat charter of ship or dry lease of aircraft is in
effect a financing arrangement and mostly constitutes a finance lease.
6.1 Treatment of Income from Leasing or Charter of Ships and
Aircraft under the Domestic Law
Income from leasing or charter of ships and aircraft will, in most cases, not
constitute freight income. As such, section 18 of the NTA and Section 21 of
the NTAA will not apply to income arising from the lease or charter of ships
or aircraft, being non-freight income. Accordingly, such income will be
taxed in accordance with the normal taxation rules in the tax laws, including
WHT deduction. However, where a tax treaty is in force, the tax treatment
of this category of income will be determined in accordance with the
applicable treaty provisions, as explained in the following paragraphs.
13

6.2 Treatment of Income from Leasing or Charter of Ships and
Aircraft where there is Tax Treaty
6.2.1. Wet Lease, Time or Voyage Charter
The profits of a company, resident in the jurisdiction of a treaty partner with
Nigeria, accruing from the charter or leasing of aircrafts or ships on time or
voyage basis, or wet lease arrangement will constitute profits from air and
shipping transportation, provided that the charter is incidental to
international traffic. Such profits will be treated in line with the Article on
shipping and air transport in that treaty, so far as such charter is solely for
international traffic.
In this regard, the income of the non-resident company will be subject to tax
on the basis of the following instances, depending on the provisions of the
specific tax treaty:
(a) Where the treaty does not allow for source State taxation: the non-
resident company will be taxable only in its home country.
(b) Where the treaty allows for source State taxation but there is
reciprocity in international traffic in a year of assessment: the foreign
airline or shipping company will not be subject to tax in Nigeria in that
year of assessment. In such a case, each country will tax its own airline
or shipping company.
(c) Where the treaty allows for source State taxation and there is no
reciprocity in international traffic in a year of assessment: the tax
payable by the non-resident in Nigeria shall be at the rate specified in
the respective tax treaty. However, where the income is derived from
only domestic routes within Nigeria, such profits will not be considered
profits derived from international traffic and would be treated as
‘business profits’ under Article 7 of the treaty. Consequently, the lease
or rental income will be assessed to tax under the relevant provision of
the domestic tax law.
Illustration 7
The Super Eagle of Nigeria has qualified for the 2026 World Cup holding in
USA and the Nigeria Football Federation has chartered the British Airways to
airlift the team to and from the USA.
Treatment:
This is a voyage charter and will qualify as international traffic under the
treaty between Nigeria and United Kingdom.
14

Illustration 8
Company A is a courier and logistic company in Nigeria. Company A has
contracted Company B, a company engaged in international shipping
transportation and a resident of the Netherlands, to transport and deliver its
goods and mails in year 2026 at various ports across the world.
Treatment:
This is a time charter and will qualify as international traffic under the tax
treaty between Nigeria and the Netherlands. This will be the case even
where, under the terms of the contract, a vessel is specifically dedicated to
the carriage of goods and mails of Company A.
NOTE:
1. Where Company B is not a company engaged in international shipping
transportation, the contract with company A will not be incidental to an
international traffic business. In that instance, income derived from the
contract will not be treated as income from international traffic but rent.
2. Issues are treated on cases-by-case basis, depending on the express
provisions of the particular tax treaty.
6.2.2. Dry Lease or Bareboat Basis
Profits of companies derived from the charter or leasing of an aircraft or ship
on bareboat basis or dry lease arrangement shall not constitute income from
air and shipping transportation (except the Agreement specifically provides
otherwise). The profits are taxed as “business profits” under relevant article
of the DTA. Consequently, the lease or rental income shall be assessed to
tax under the relevant provision of the domestic tax law, including
withholding tax and value added tax.
The lessee in Nigeria may claim capital allowance in respect of the asset.
Illustration 9:
YBM Airlines, an incorporated company in Nigeria, wants to expand its air
transport operations and has taken a wet lease of one aircraft from ADK
Airways, a resident of Fantasia, for a period of 5 years to increase its daily
flights between Abuja and Lagos routes. YBM would be required to pay ADK
at quarterly intervals based on agreed daily rates for the duration of the
lease.
YBM is also required to take on the insurance on passengers, baggage, cargo
or mail, all operating costs in connection to the aircraft (or reimburse ADK for
it if incurred by ADK) which includes the fuel and lubricants, landing and
parking fees, ground handling, carbon emission charges, passenger and crew
in-flight catering etc., and pay a security deposit before the lease starts, by
virtue of the terms of the agreement. YBM in addition will ensure that the
15

Aircraft is free and clear of all liens, charges and encumbrances that have
arisen during the wet lease period.
However, ADK will take care of crew expenses and any cost relating to loss
or damage to the aircraft including replacement of the aircraft so far as it is
not from gross negligence or willful misconduct by YBM. Fantasia does not
have a treaty with Nigeria.
Treatment:
ADK establishes a permanent establishment (PE) in Nigeria through the
provision of its aircraft and crew, thereby creating a taxable presence, which
will make it liable for corporate income tax on profits attributable to the PE.
The income earned by ADK will constitute non-freight lease income, which
will not be classified as income from air transport operations. The taxation
rules for non-resident shipping and air transport under the NTA and NTAA
will not apply to this arrangement, and ADK will be required to render returns
as a non-resident deriving income from Nigeria.
WHT applies to all payments made by YBM to ADK, which when remitted to
the Service, is advance payment of its income tax liability, and will not be
considered a final tax.
Illustration 10:
Fantasia is a treaty partner of Nigeria and one of its resident companies,
ADK, flies purely international routes between Nigeria and Fantasia. The
treaty between Nigeria and Fantasia allows for source State taxation where
there is no reciprocity. In its efforts to expand its operations to international
routes between Nigeria and Fantasia, YBM Airlines, a Nigerian company
entered into a of 5-year joint operation agreement with ADK. All other facts
and conditions stated in Illustration 7 above are assumed to be the same.
Treatment:
Both ADK and YBM derives income from international traffic under the joint
arrangement. As such, the conditions for reciprocity under the tax treaties
of Nigeria is met.
Consequently, each country will tax its airlines and the profits of ADK will not
be taxable in Nigeria, although the treaty allows for source State taxation.
Illustration 11:
Fantasia is a treaty partner of Nigeria and one of its resident companies, ADK
flies purely international routes between Nigeria and Fantasia. The treaty
between Nigeria and Fantasia allows for source State taxation where there is
16

no reciprocity. In its efforts to expand its domestic operations, especially in
the routes between Abuja and Enugu, YBM Airlines, a Nigerian company
entered into a wet lease agreement with ADK for a period of 5 years. All
other facts and conditions stated in Illustration 7 above are assumed to be
the same.
Treatment:
ADK derives income from international traffic while YBM does not. As such,
the conditions for reciprocity under the tax treaties of Nigeria has not been
met. Consequently, Nigeria will tax the profits of ADK at the rate specified in
the relevant tax treaty, if the treaty allows for source State taxation. While
the income of YBM will be subject to tax in Nigeria in accordance with the
relevant tax law. The income of ADK taxable in Nigeria will include the income
from wet lease of aircraft, which will be treated as non-freight income, and
not income from international traffic
7.0 Income from employment exercised aboard a ship or
aircraft
Income covered under this paragraph includes income from employment
exercised aboard a ship or aircraft as part of the crew or in the course of
usual operation of the ship or aircraft. Examples of such activities include
disc jockeys, expedition leaders, hosts and hostesses, shore excursion
managers, water sports instructors, fitness directors, medical staff,
bartenders, information technology staff, casino staff, entertainers etc.
exercised aboard a cruise ship.
7.1 Tax Treatment of Income from employment under the
Domestic Law
7.1.1 Resident individual
An individual who is a resident of Nigeria, whether a master, pilot, crew or
ground-staff is liable to tax in Nigeria on all income derived from within and
outside Nigeria. Employment income, including compensations, bonuses,
premiums and benefits, irrespective of where the income is earned or the
employment is exercised and whether or not the income is brought into or
received in Nigeria will be liable to tax in Nigeria. This is regardless of where
the employer is tax resident.
7.1.2 Non-resident individual
Employment income of a non-resident individual, including a master, pilot,
member of the crew or ground staff, is not liable to tax in Nigeria except
where the employment is wholly or partly exercised in Nigeria, and the
income is not taxable in the country of tax residence of the employee.
17

Where the payer is a resident person, tax will be deducted when the
payment of the emolument is made, but subject to refund upon
presentation of evidence of taxation in country of tax residence.
7.2 Tax treatment of income from employment where there is tax
treaty
7.2.1 Where the ship or aircraft operates in international traffic
Where an individual exercises employment aboard a ship or aircraft in
international traffic or serves as a member of the regular complement
on that vessel, the income may be subject to tax in Nigeria. Such profits
will be treated in line with the Article on dependent personal service or
income from employment.
The tax treatment may defer, depending on the treaty provisions. The
following are possible treatments:
(i) Shared taxation that allows for taxation in the resident state of the
operator of the ship or aircraft (residence of employer) or the place of
effective management of the ship or aircraft: Nigeria will tax in
accordance with its domestic law if the ship or aircraft is operated or
effectively managed by a resident of Nigeria, as the case may be.
Nigeria will also have taxing right if the employee is its resident.
(ii) Exclusive taxation which allows for taxation only in the country of
residence of employee: Nigeria will be able to tax its residence and will not
have a taxing right in respect of non-residents.
(iii) Exclusive taxation which allows for taxation only in the country of
residence of employer or the place of effective management of the ship
or aircraft: Nigeria will have taxing right only if the ship or aircraft is
operated or effectively managed by a resident of Nigeria, as the case
may be.
7.2.2 Where the ship or aircraft does not operate in international
traffic
The income from employment will be treated in accordance with the rules
stated in paragraph 7.1 above, except that in the case of non-resident, the
condition for source state taxation under the Article on income from
employment must be met before Nigeria can exercise a right of taxation
under the domestic law.
8.0 Taxation of Foreign Ships or Vessels Lifting Crude Oil from
Nigerian Territorial Waters
One of the common features of the oil industry in Nigeria is that crude oil is
18

often sold to foreign buyers “Free on Board” origin (“FOB origin”), also
sometimes phrased as "FOB shipping" or "FOB shipping point". This means
that the foreign or non-resident buyers are responsible for the arrangement
and payment for vessels for the transportation of the crude oil from Nigeria.
Usually, the shipping companies contracted for the transportation of the
crude are non-residents and payments to them are made by the non-
resident buyers of the crude oil.
The tax treatment of income derived from the carriage of crude oil from
Nigeria follows the same principles applicable to non-resident companies
engaged in shipping operations.
Consequently, a vessel that carries crude oil, gas, petroleum products or any
other item from Nigeria is liable to tax in Nigeria, irrespective of where or
with whom the carriage contract was executed, subject to the application
of the respective tax treaty rules, where applicable.
8.1 Income from Ancillary Services
8.1.1 Under the Domestic Law
The special provisions governing the taxation of shipping and air transport
operations do not extend to non-freight income, including income arising
from demurrage and detention, local charges, stevedoring, clearing and
forwarding, cargo handling, container leasing, storage, agency services,
and similar activities. Where a foreign shipping or air transport company
carries on any of these non-freight activities in Nigeria, the profits derived
therefrom are subject to tax in Nigeria in accordance with the general
provisions applicable to income derived from Nigeria by non-resident
companies.
These ancillary services are liable to Value Added Tax (VAT). The non-
resident airline or shipping company must therefore include VAT in the
invoice and a Nigerian resident to whom the services are provided are
required to withhold the VAT and remit it to the Service in accordance with
the extant tax laws. Where the Service has appointed a non-resident
shipping or airline as an agent for the collection of VAT, the taxable person
will not be required to withhold the VAT except when the appointed agent
has failed to collect the VAT.
9.0 Remittance of funds out of Nigeria
Remittance of funds out of Nigeria, by a foreign company engaged in shipping
or airline business, requires a Clearance Certificate issued by the Service. The
certificate is to show that relevant tax has been paid on the income from which
the fund is generated or that the income is not liable to Nigerian tax.
19

It is an offence to make remittance without obtaining the relevant Clearance
Certificate, which is liable to penalty under the provisions of section 127 of the
NTAA.
